display.title: Parshas Toldos: Turning the Yetzer Hara's Tricks Around
display.summary_short: From Rivkah's twins, the Alter Rebbe's lesson about the two inclinations, and a story of a hotel keeper saved in court by the very condition that made him liable.
display.summary_long: Why does the Shema say to love Hashem with "levavcha", with two hearts? Chazal explain that we serve Hashem with both the good and the evil inclination. Looking at the start of Parshas Toldos, the storyteller explains why Rivkah was troubled when the baby seemed to push toward both a yeshiva and a place of idol worship, and why she was calm once she learned she was carrying twins. The Alter Rebbe uses this to teach that stray thoughts during davening come from the yetzer hara, and they actually show that the davening is good. Hashem gave us a yetzer hara so we can grow by overcoming it, and like Rabbi Zusha, who learned seven lessons from a thief, we can even turn its ideas around: steal time from play for learning. The story: three partners leave their money with a hotel keeper on condition he return it only to all three. One partner tricks him and runs off with it, and the court makes the hotel keeper pay. His Rav argues that he is ready to pay, but only to all three together, as agreed, so the very condition that condemned him saves him.
display.lesson: The yetzer hara is there to make us stronger; we can use its own tricks to serve Hashem better.
